# Use a stable, common base image suitable for HPC applications
FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Set DEBIAN_FRONTEND to noninteractive to prevent prompts during package installation
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Install build essentials, dependencies for LAMMPS, MPI, and required certificates in a single layer
# FIX: Added python3, which is a required dependency for the modern LAMMPS CMake build system.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    cmake \
    git \
    python3 \
    ca-certificates \
    openmpi-bin \
    libopenmpi-dev \
    libfftw3-dev \
    libgomp1 \
    # Clean up apt cache to reduce image size
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Set a temporary working directory for the source code and build process
WORKDIR /tmp/build

# Clone the latest branch of LAMMPS source code from GitHub.
# --depth 1 creates a shallow clone, which is faster and smaller.
RUN git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/lammps/lammps.git .

# Build LAMMPS from source using CMake
# This process is combined into a single RUN command to optimize layer usage
RUN mkdir cmake-build && cd cmake-build && \
    # Configure the build for a release version with MPI and the REAXFF package
    cmake ../cmake \
    -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
    -D BUILD_MPI=yes \
    -D PKG_REAXFF=yes && \
    # Compile the code using all available processor cores
    make -j$(nproc) && \
    # Copy the main LAMMPS executable 'lmp' to a directory on the system's PATH
    cp lmp /usr/local/bin/

# Configure OpenMPI for containerized environments
# These settings improve compatibility when running as root and on container networks
RUN echo "btl_vader_single_copy_mechanism = none" >> /etc/openmpi/openmpi-mca-params.conf && \
    echo "btl_tcp_if_exclude = lo,docker0" >> /etc/openmpi/openmpi-mca-params.conf && \
    echo "orte_base_help_aggregate = 0" >> /etc/openmpi/openmpi-mca-params.conf

# Create the final application directory and set it as the WORKDIR
WORKDIR /app

# Copy the example input files for the ReaxFF HNS benchmark from the source tree
RUN cp /tmp/build/examples/reaxff/HNS/* .

# Clean up the build directory to minimize the final image size
RUN rm -rf /tmp/build

flux-minicluster-manifest.item:
# This MiniCluster manifest is designed to run a LAMMPS ReaxFF simulation
# on a single AWS CPU-based Kubernetes node using the Flux Operator.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # A descriptive name for the MiniCluster instance.
  name: lammps-reax-aws-cpu
  # The namespace where the MiniCluster will be deployed.
  namespace: default
spec:
  # Specifies the number of pods in the MiniCluster. Set to 1 for a single-node run.
  size: 1

  # Total number of MPI tasks to run. Flux will start this many tasks across the cluster.
  tasks: 1

  # If true, pod logs are streamed to the operator log.
  logging:
    strict: true

  # Do not delete the pods when the job is complete. Useful for debugging.
  cleanup: false

  # Define the single container that will run the LAMMPS simulation.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:lammps-reax
      
      # The command to execute. The Flux Operator will prepend `flux run -n <tasks> ...` to this command.
      # This runs the LAMMPS executable `lmp` with the specified input file `in.reaxff.hns`.
      command: lmp -v x 2 -v y 2 -v z 2 -in ./in.reaxff.hns -nocite
      
      # This is not a launcher-only pod; the main workload runs directly in this container.
      launcher: false

updates.reason: The previous attempt with 512 tasks on a 64-core node resulted in a 26s wall time, indicating severe performance degradation from CPU oversubscription. This attempt matches the task count to the available physical cores (64) on the hpc7g.16xlarge instance and adjusts the processor decomposition grid to 4x4x4. This should significantly reduce scheduling and communication overhead, leading to a much faster wall time.

Achieved an excellent 6s wall time on a 64-core ARM instance (hpc7g.16xlarge). This attempt will test the best available x86 alternative, the 48-core AMD c7a.12xlarge. By matching tasks to cores (48), this experiment will determine if superior per-core performance on the x86 architecture can overcome the core count advantage of the ARM instance.

Optimization is complete. A minimum wall time of 6 seconds was achieved by correctly matching MPI tasks to the available CPU cores. This optimal time was reproduced on the two most powerful available instances (64-core ARM hpc7g.16xlarge and 48-core AMD c7a.12xlarge), indicating that the performance limit for this workload on a single node has been reached. Further attempts are unlikely to yield significant improvements.
